newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Twyla Tharp on the road again with new troupe.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Twyla Tharp on the road again with new troupe.

text.p: Twyla Tharp is back on the road with her own troupe for the first time since 1988, giving one of the doyennes of modern dance the busy life she says she missed.

"Tharp!" is the choreographer's first troupe since she disbanded her company eight years ago to work as a visiting choreographer for England's Royal Ballet, the Paris Opera Ballet and the American Ballet Theatre, among others. During that time Tharp, now 54, developed an extensive repertoire that included dances for Mikhail Baryshnikov, but she told Reuters the years working with large companies "didn't feed into the future," so she left.

"I want to work all the time and it's obvious for a person who works as much as I do that it was necessary for me to leave (the American Ballet Theatre)," said Tharp, whose new troupe is a showcase for her range of dance styles developed over the years since her first company in 1965.
It operates without grants or donations from private or public sources. "The notion that the arts had to be subsidised was always a rather distasteful one to me," she said.

Tharp's work ethic is legendary and was a theme in one of the three pieces recently performed on the first leg of her troupe's U.S. tour, which ended in November. The second leg begins in January and "Tharp!" may tour in Europe next autumn.

"66" is her Vaudevillean ode to the road her family took from Indiana to Rialto, California, where her parents opened a drive-in movie theatre in the 1950s. Two of her dancers, encapsulated in black styrofoam, performed as the tires.

"The highway put my parents' four kids through college," Tharp said. "It's a nod to the opportunities that are available in democratic America. It makes one want to say thank you. It is a reason to work -- to say thank you."

Tharp looked less the workaholic than a proud mother at the conclusion of a recent Chicago performance. With her grayish-blond hair pulled in a loose ponytail, she strode onstage applauding her dancers as much as basking in the applause from the audience.

She said deciding which dancers to select for her new troupe came down to choosing 13 who were classically trained yet comfortable with their bodies -- and that quality was evident to her in "the minute-and-a-half it takes them to come through the door and put their bag down on the floor."

The two other dances performed on the recent tour, "Sweet Fields," which harkens back to Tharp's Quaker roots in her native Indiana, and "Heroes," her collaboration with American composer Philip Glass, were much more evocative and lyrical.

Tharp's dance to Glass' six-movement symphony, which was inspired by the album "Heroes" by rockers David Bowie and Brian Eno, displayed the same athletic, hyperkinetic moves as their 1986 collaborative masterpiece, "The Upper Room." The work climaxed with a struggle among a trio of male protagonists who, standing in a wall of defiance, let a woman fall after she hurled herself toward their waiting arms.

Strains of "The Upper Room" could be seen and heard in the piece, but the climax in "Heroes" was less triumphant and majestic, an aspect of the work that its creator acknowledged. "I had a friend who said we might as well say 'Heroes' is 'The Lower Room,'" Tharp said. "The energy is geared out in 'The Upper Room' while with 'Heroes' you are moving with a lot of resistance."

The lyrical movement of the white-outfitted ensemble in "Sweet Fields" echoed the accompanying hymnal music of William Billings, an 18th century American composer. "Heroes" and "Sweet Fields" both possessed the uncanny quality of embodying the music, allowing the viewer almost to see the accompanying polyphonic music through Tharp's masterful use of movement.

The symphony's ostinatos, or repeated musical pitches, were mirrored in Tharp's choreography, as the chorus reproduced her signature gestures such as flex-footed kicks, nonchalant strolls off-stage and running in tight circles.
